title: Design ticket booking without overselling
summary: An on-sale where two million fans want fifty thousand seats: seat holds with expiry, optimistic concurrency versus SELECT FOR UPDATE, idempotent payment and a waiting room.

steps.title: Requirements and estimates
body: **The ask:** fans pick seats for an event and pay. Big events sell out in minutes.
| Kind | Requirement |
| Functional | browse the seat map; hold seats while paying (10 minutes); pay; receive tickets |
| Non-functional | **never sell a seat twice** (correctness beats availability here); fair to fans who came first; survive the on-sale spike |
| Out of scope | dynamic pricing, resale marketplace, bot detection (mention it) |
```text
seats        50,000 for one event
fans         2 M arrive within the first minutes of the on-sale
seat map     2 M x refreshes: tens of thousands of reads / s, all for one event
bookings     at most 25,000 (2 seats each): small writes, but all on the same rows
The volume of **writes** is tiny. The problem is **contention**: everyone wants the same few thousand front
seats at the same second, and reads of one event's seat map are a hot key.

steps.prompt: The database can confirm 500 bookings per second, and each booking is 2 seats. What is the fastest the 50,000 seats can sell out?
steps.explain: 50,000 seats / 2 = 25,000 bookings; / 500 per second = 50 s. Letting 2 M fans hammer the database in those 50 seconds gains nothing: the rate is fixed. Admitting fans at a controlled rate (a waiting room) gives the same sell-out time with a calm database.

steps.title: Data model and the design
body: ```sql
CREATE TABLE seats (
event_id        bigint,
seat_id         text,
status          text NOT NULL,        -- available | held | sold
holder          bigint,               -- user holding or owning it
hold_expires_at timestamptz,
version         int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_id)
```text
fans --> CDN (seat map snapshot, refreshed every few s)
--> waiting room (queue tokens, admits N fans / s) --> booking API --> seats DB (one event per shard)
|--> payment provider (idempotency key)
'--> hold sweeper (releases expired holds)
- A **hold** reserves the seat for 10 minutes while the fan pays. Expired holds count as available again.
- The seat map that 2 M people refresh is served from a **cached snapshot**; only the hold itself must hit the
database and be exact.

steps.prompt: Two fans both read the seat at version 3, then both try a conditional update. What does this print?
steps.explain: This is `UPDATE ... WHERE version = 3`: the first one matches and bumps the version, so the second matches zero rows. The application reads the affected-row count and tells the second fan the seat is gone.

steps.title: Optimistic or pessimistic?
body: | | Optimistic: version check | Pessimistic: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` |
| How | `UPDATE seats SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE seat_id = $1 AND version = $2`; 0 rows means someone else won | lock the row in a transaction, check, update, commit |
| Contention | losers fail fast and retry with fresh data | losers **wait** for the lock, holding connections |
| Good for | a specific seat chosen by the fan | "any 2 seats in section B": `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 2` hands different rows to concurrent buyers |
| Danger | none for correctness; many retries under heavy contention | lock waits and deadlocks (lock rows in a fixed order) |
Both are correct. What is **not** correct is reading the status, checking it in application code, and then
writing without a condition: two requests both see "available" and both write "held".

steps.prompt: Complete the hold so it only succeeds if nobody changed the seat since the fan read it, and an expired hold counts as free.
code: SET status = 'held', holder = $3, hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes', version = version + 1
steps.explain: The version guard makes it a compare-and-set. The application must check that exactly 1 row was affected; 0 rows means the seat was taken or changed, so show the fan the fresh state.

prompt: **Symptom first.** From the on-sale postmortem: "312 seats were sold twice." The booking code:
var status = await db.QuerySingleAsync<string>("SELECT status FROM seats WHERE seat_id = @id", new { id });
await db.ExecuteAsync("UPDATE seats SET status = 'held', holder = @user WHERE seat_id = @id", new { id, user });
Why did it oversell, and what is the fix?
options: Check-then-act race: two requests read 'available' before either wrote. Make the write conditional (WHERE status/version, check rows affected) or lock with FOR UPDATE
The database lost writes under load: add a replica
The cache served a stale seat map: lower its TTL
The holds expired too early: make them 20 minutes
steps.explain: Under PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED level the two statements are separate, so both requests pass the check. A stale seat map only changes what fans click; the database write must be the guard.

steps.title: Payment, holds and the waiting room
body: - **Idempotent payment.** Create the order first (`PENDING`), then charge with an **idempotency key** derived from
the order id. A retry after a timeout returns the original charge instead of charging twice; payment
providers widely support such keys.
- **Confirm in one transaction:** seat `sold` and order `PAID` together, and only if the hold is still yours.
- **Expired holds** are free by the rule in the `WHERE` clause; a sweeper tidies them for the seat map.
- **Waiting room.** At the on-sale, fans get a queue position (randomised among those who arrived before the
start, then first come first served) and are admitted at a rate the booking path can take. That turns a
stampede into a steady flow, and nobody gets an error page.

lines: Pass the waiting room and get an admission token
Hold the seat with a conditional update (version check)
Create the order as PENDING with an idempotency key
Charge the card through the payment provider with that key
Mark the seat sold and the order PAID in one transaction

steps.title: Seat holds with compare-and-set
prompt: Write a class `SeatMap` (time passed in, in ms):
- `SeatMap(IEnumerable<string> seatIds, long holdMs)`: every seat starts `available` at version `0`.
- `string Status(string seat, long now)`: `"available"`, `"held"` or `"sold"`. A hold whose expiry has passed
- `bool Hold(string seat, string user, int expectedVersion, long now)`: succeeds only if the version is still
`expectedVersion` **and** the seat is available at `now`. On success it is held by `user` until `now + holdMs`
and the version goes up by one.
- `bool Confirm(string seat, string user, long now)`: succeeds only if the seat is held by this `user` and the hold
has not expired. It becomes `sold` and the version goes up by one.
starter: public string Status(string seat, long now) => "available";
public bool Hold(string seat, string user, int expectedVersion, long now) => false;
public bool Confirm(string seat, string user, long now) => false;
solution: record Seat(string State, string? User, long Expires, int Version);
foreach (var id in seatIds) seats[id] = new Seat("available", null, 0, 0);
public string Status(string seat, long now)
public bool Hold(string seat, string user, int expectedVersion, long now)
if (s.Version != expectedVersion || Status(seat, now) != "available") return false;
seats[seat] = new Seat("held", user, now + holdMs, s.Version + 1);
public bool Confirm(string seat, string user, long now)
if (s.State != "held" || s.User != user || now >= s.Expires) return false;
seats[seat] = s with { State = "sold", Version = s.Version + 1 };
hints: Keep one small record per seat: state, holder, expiry and version.
`Hold` checks the version and `Status(seat, now) == "available"`; `Confirm` checks holder, state and expiry.
template: Dojo.Eq("new seats are at version 0", 0, dojoM.Version("A1"));
Dojo.Eq("bo read version 0 too: his hold fails", false, dojoM.Hold("A1", "bo", 0, 0));
Dojo.Eq("the hold bumped the version", 1, dojoM.Version("A1"));
Dojo.Eq("bo with fresh data still cannot take a held seat", false, dojoM.Hold("A1", "bo", 1, 1000));
Dojo.Eq("bo cannot confirm ana's hold", false, dojoM.Confirm("A1", "bo", 2000));
Dojo.Eq("a sold seat stays sold", false, dojoM.Hold("A1", "bo", 2, 900_000));
Dojo.Eq("the hold expires after 10 minutes", "available", dojoM.Status("A2", 600_000));
Dojo.Eq("an expired hold cannot be confirmed", false, dojoM.Confirm("A2", "ana", 600_000));
Dojo.Eq("bo takes the expired seat", true, dojoM.Hold("A2", "bo", 1, 600_000));

steps.title: Build it: absorb the on-sale burst
prompt: In the **System design board**, an on-sale sends a burst of writes that the database cannot take synchronously.
Put a queue and workers in the write path (no more workers than partitions), answer quickly, keep the database
under its goal and drain the backlog in time.
steps.explain: A queue turns a burst into a backlog. The database then works at its own steady rate, and the drain time (backlog / (consume rate - arrival rate)) tells you whether fans wait seconds or minutes.
